summary: A country in the western Balkan Peninsula made up of three main peoples, the Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, which went through a devastating war in the 1990s and is now composed of two entities.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: After the Ottoman Empire conquered Bosnia in 1463, many local residents gradually converted to Islam, for reasons including that conversion reduced the tax burden and allowed entry into the imperial bureaucracy, and that the region already had the 'Bosnian Church', which was not recognized by the Catholic or Orthodox churches. Islam developed a distinctive culture in the towns of Bosnia, represented by the Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque in Sarajevo, built in the 16th century. Today's Muslims are mostly Bosniaks, who suffered mass killings in the war of 1992-1995, such as the Srebrenica massacre of 1995.

ranking.name: Serbian Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Serbian Orthodox believers are mainly Serbs, concentrated in eastern and northern Bosnia, today's Republika Srpska. The influence of Byzantium and Serbia in the Middle Ages made Orthodoxy take root in the east, and the Patriarchate of Peć, restored in 1557 during Ottoman times, also governed the Orthodox believers of Bosnia. In Bosnia religion and ethnic identity overlap closely, and Serbian Orthodoxy is the core of Serb identity.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholic believers are mainly Croats, concentrated in Herzegovina in the southwest and in the central region. Franciscan friars preached in Bosnia in the Middle Ages, and in the Ottoman period the Franciscans were the only Catholic order permitted to remain, and they protected the Catholic community. In 1981 apparitions of the Virgin Mary were reported at Medjugorje in Herzegovina, attracting large numbers of pilgrims, but the Vatican has long remained cautious about it.

ranking.name: No religion and others
ranking.description: The share of the non-religious and of other religions is very low, consisting mainly of city dwellers who grew up in the socialist Yugoslav period (1945-1992) and were affected by secularization, together with a few Jews and Protestants. The war of 1992-1995 made religious and ethnic identity even more tightly bound, so only about 2 percent identify as having no religion.

religion.background: Medieval Bosnia lay between the two great powers of Catholicism and Orthodoxy, and an independent 'Bosnian Church' appeared there. After the Ottoman conquest in 1463 Islam gradually spread, forming a situation of coexisting Muslims, Orthodox and Catholics, and the Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 also moved to Sarajevo, which led to its being called the 'Jerusalem of Europe'. In 1878 Austria-Hungary took over, and after 1918 it was incorporated into Yugoslavia. In the Bosnian War of 1992-1995 religion became the marker of ethnic division, and the country's politics after the war also divides power along ethnic and religious lines.

language.official: The official languages are Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian.

ranking.name: Bosnian
ranking.description: Bosnian is the language used by the Bosniaks (Muslims), and in grammar and vocabulary it is almost identical to Serbian and Croatian, all derived from the same South Slavic language, collectively called 'Serbo-Croatian' in the Yugoslav period. After the breakup of Yugoslavia and the Bosnian War in the 1990s, each people politicized the names of their languages, and Bosnian stresses the retention of Turkish and Arabic loanwords from the Ottoman period.

ranking.name: Serbian
ranking.description: Serbian is used mainly by Serbs, concentrated in Republika Srpska, and both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets are used. After the Dayton Agreement of 1995 ended the war, Bosnia was divided into two entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, and Republika Srpska uses Serbian as its main language, with the Cyrillic alphabet as the official script.

ranking.name: Croatian
ranking.description: Croatian is used by the Croats, concentrated in Herzegovina in the southwest, and is the same as the standard language of neighboring Croatia. Croatian differs very little from Bosnian and Serbian and the three are mutually intelligible, but after the war the schools of each people used different textbooks, resulting in the phenomenon of 'two schools under one roof'.

language.history: After the South Slavs moved into the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries, the Bosnian region used the Shtokavian dialect of South Slavic, and in the Middle Ages used a script called 'Bosnian Cyrillic'. Ottoman rule from 1463 led the local language to absorb a great deal of Turkish, Arabic and Persian vocabulary. The Vienna Literary Agreement of 1850 in the mid-19th century established a Serbo-Croatian standard on the basis of the Shtokavian dialect, which was the common language in the Yugoslav period. After the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, the three peoples named their languages Bosnian, Serbian and Croatian respectively, and the three are all official languages.

ranking.name: Ćevapi
ranking.description: Ground beef or a mixture of beef and lamb is shaped into small sausages and charcoal-grilled; a portion is usually ten pieces, served in flatbread with raw onion and kajmak cream cheese.
ranking.history: Ćevapi derives from the Ottoman kebab tradition, and the name comes from a diminutive form of the Turkish 'kebap'; after the 16th century it became popular in the Balkans with Ottoman rule. The old town of Sarajevo, Baščaršija, has been a commercial center since Ottoman times, and there are still many specialized ćevapi shops (ćevabdžinica). It is regarded as Bosnia's national dish and is also the representative food by which Bosnian emigrants abroad remember their homeland after the war.

ranking.name: Burek
ranking.description: Hand-stretched thin dough is wrapped around ground beef and onion, rolled into a long strip or spiral and baked; the crust is crisp and the filling juicy, and it is often eaten with yogurt.
ranking.history: Burek derives from the Ottoman 'börek' pastry and came to Bosnia with Ottoman rule after the 15th century. In Bosnia only the one with meat filling is called 'burek', the cheese one is called 'sirnica' and the spinach one 'zeljanica', and this strict naming is often proudly emphasized by the locals. It is the star of breakfast and street snacks, and traditional bakeries (buregdžinica) usually start baking early in the morning.

ranking.name: Bosanski Lonac
ranking.description: Large pieces of beef or lamb are layered in a clay pot with many vegetables such as cabbage, potato, carrot and tomato, water is added, and it is slowly stewed for a long time.
ranking.history: Bosnian pot is a rural dish with a long history, said to originate with medieval miners and farmers, who put the ingredients in a clay pot and left it by the stove or in the ashes to stew slowly in the morning, so that they could eat when they came off work. This one-pot dish does not need much attention and can use all kinds of seasonal vegetables. Today it is a classic dish of Bosnian family winter meals and often appears at festivals.
ranking.imageCredit: Kami at German Wikipedia・Public domain・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Begova Čorba
ranking.description: A thick soup stewed from chicken, okra and root vegetables such as carrot and celery, thickened with egg yolk and sour cream; the texture is smooth and the taste mild.
ranking.history: The name 'Begova čorba' comes from the Ottoman noble title 'beg' (bey), meaning that this was a fine soup enjoyed by noble families in the past. Okra is very common in Ottoman cooking and came to the Balkans with the expansion of the empire. Today it is the starter soup at important occasions such as Bosnian weddings and Eid al-Fitr, and is also the signature dish of traditional restaurants.

ranking.name: Tufahija
ranking.description: Apples are cored and poached in sugar syrup, the center is filled with a walnut stuffing, and a layer of whipped cream is added on top; it is eaten cold, sweet but not cloying, with a fresh aroma.
ranking.history: Tufahija originated in the Ottoman Empire, and its name comes from the Turkish 'tuffah' (apple, from Arabic); after the 16th century it came to Bosnia with Ottoman rule. It was once a dessert of the Ottoman court and noble families, and later spread among the Muslim families of Bosnia. Today it is representative of the traditional dessert shops of Sarajevo and is often enjoyed with Bosnian coffee.
